name: חיבור שברים – מונים לינאריים ומכנים מספריים (באנגלית)

functions.name: igcd2
functions.body: if q=0 then abs(p) else igcd2(q,mod(p,q))

questiontext:
Express the following as a single fraction in its lowest terms:

\[ \frac{{CT:0}}{{CT:1}}+\frac{{CT:2}}{{CT:3}}. \]

[[input:ans]]
[[validation:ans]]
generalfeedback:
Outline: Bring both fractions to the lowest common denominator, add, open the brackets in the numerator, then cancel any common factor.
Step 1 — The common denominator
When adding fractions with linear expressions the method remains the same. First, find a suitable common denominator: the lowest common multiple of the denominators is \(\operatorname{lcm}({{CT:1}},{{CT:3}})={{CT:4}}\). Expand each fraction to this denominator and add the fractions. In this example:

\[ \frac{{CT:0}}{{CT:1}}+\frac{{CT:2}}{{CT:3}} = \frac{{CT:5}}{{CT:4}}+\frac{{CT:6}}{{CT:4}} = \frac{{CT:7}}{{CT:4}} \]

Step 2 — Open the brackets and collect like terms
After adding, collect the 'like terms':

\[ {{CT:7}}={{CT:8}}+{{CT:9}}={{CT:10}} \]

Step 3 — Lowest terms
Cancel any common factors from the numerator and the denominator. [[if test="{{CT:15}}"]]The numerator and the denominator have the common factor \({{CT:11}}\); cancel it:

\[ \frac{{{CT:10}}}{{{CT:4}}}=\frac{{{CT:11}}\left({{CT:12}}\right)}{{{CT:11}}\cdot {{CT:13}}} \]

Now nothing else cancels, so the fraction is in its lowest terms:[[else]]The numerator and the denominator have no common factor other than \(1\), so the fraction is already in its lowest terms:[[/if]]

\[ \frac{{CT:0}}{{CT:1}}+\frac{{CT:2}}{{CT:3}} = \frac{{CT:5}}{{CT:4}}+\frac{{CT:6}}{{CT:4}} = \frac{{CT:7}}{{CT:4}} = {{CT:14}}. \]

on_true.feedback: Your answer is not in its simplest form but is otherwise correct.
You cannot simply add the numerator and denominator when adding fractions. Instead use the general rule: \(\frac{a}{c}+\frac{b}{d} = \frac{ad+bc}{cd} \)
